content: Community health workers, even with minimal training, have been successfully involved in providing curative and preventive care in various health sectors, including maternal and child health services, malaria diagnosis and treatment, and tuberculosis (TB) care. This demonstrates their potential to contribute to the HIV care continuum, including testing, treatment, and ongoing care. The use of lay providers to distribute antiretroviral therapy (ART) offers several public health benefits. These include increasing the number of service providers to address shortages in healthcare personnel, reducing clinic congestion, and bringing services closer to communities, which improves retention in care. However, in settings where the supply and management of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are unreliable, expanding distribution sites outside health facilities could exacerbate stock management challenges. Studies included in systematic reviews have not yet evaluated the inclusion of individuals with comorbidities or children in these models. While the recommendations are applicable to these populations, necessary dose adjustments for children as they grow can be safely managed during clinic visits, with maintenance treatment provided at the community level. The initial implementation of community-based ART distribution may involve increased costs for training and other associated expenses. However, studies have shown that patients face significantly higher costs when traveling to centralized health services to collect medication. For example, a study in Uganda found that the cost of hospital-based care was three times higher than home-based care. Task shifting, which involves delegating responsibilities to less specialized health workers, has been shown to improve linkage to care, treatment adherence, and the capacity of HIV programs to address shortages of professional health workers. Strengthening relationships between people living with HIV and their communities can empower individuals and reduce stigma. In Malawi, community members were hired as pharmacy attendants to pre-package and distribute ARV drugs, which reduced waiting times, spaced out clinic visits, and alleviated the workload of health providers. Successful task-shifting programs require initial and ongoing training, mentoring, supportive supervision, and administrative planning. National regulatory frameworks and policies may need to be revised to allow new cadres of health workers to perform these tasks. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all health workers, including lay providers, be adequately remunerated, as reliance on volunteerism alone is unsustainable. Trained and supervised non-laboratory staff, including laypeople, can safely perform blood sample collection using finger-prick methods, which increases access to essential diagnostics and decentralizes HIV care. As HIV treatment and care have expanded over the past decade, in-service training has played a critical role in rapidly upgrading the skills of healthcare providers. Countries should also establish systems for continuing education, including clinical mentoring and supportive supervision, to keep pace with evolving knowledge in HIV care and treatment. Decentralizing HIV treatment and care reduces waiting times at health facilities and brings services closer to patients' homes. It also strengthens community engagement by linking community-based interventions with health facilities, improving access to services, care-seeking behavior, and retention in care. People living with HIV and affected communities play a vital role in providing HIV testing, treatment, care, and support. In maternal and child health settings, ART should be initiated and maintained for eligible pregnant and postpartum women and infants, with linkage to ongoing HIV care. Integrated services in these settings improve ART uptake and adherence during pregnancy and reduce stigma. However, not all maternal and child health facilities may have the capacity to provide long-term HIV treatment and care, necessitating careful planning for transitioning patients to chronic HIV care. In settings with a high burden of HIV and TB, ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care. Similarly, TB treatment can be provided in HIV care settings where a TB diagnosis has been made. These integrated approaches improve ART uptake and timeliness, although data on mortality and TB treatment success remain inconsistent. For people living with HIV who inject drugs, ART should be initiated and maintained in settings providing opioid substitution therapy (OST). OST, combined with psychosocial support, improves HIV treatment outcomes and should be accessible in prisons and other closed settings. However, OST should not be a prerequisite for initiating or maintaining ART. Integrating sexually transmitted infection (STI) and family planning services within HIV care settings can expand access to these services. Women living with HIV often have higher unmet needs for family planning services and experience high rates of unintended pregnancies. Adolescent-friendly family planning services should be prioritized, as adolescent women are more likely to have unintentional pregnancies and higher mother-to-child transmission rates. Integrated service delivery is cost-effective and leads to economies of scale. For example, integrating family planning into HIV care in Kenya was found to be feasible, inexpensive, and cost-effective. However, more research is needed to evaluate the delivery of STI services in HIV care settings, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. In conclusion, decentralizing and integrating HIV services, task-shifting, and involving community health workers and lay providers can improve access, retention, and adherence to care.
